newsitem.title: CHINA: Hong Kong's new troops - Look but don't touch.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong's new troops - Look but don't touch.

text.p: Look but don't touch seems the unspoken rule as Hong Kong begins the long process of getting to know China again after 156 years of British colonial rule.
Moments after two Chinese sentries took up their new posts at Hong Kong's Prince of Wales barracks on Tuesday, a crowd of residents and tourists surged forward to take souvenir snapshots of them.
For days British Black Watch soldiers occupying the same duty spot in the run-up to Hong Kong's handover to China had been similarly mobbed.

But where the British troops reluctantly allowed themselves to be manhandled by grandparents and teenage girls, who moved them around like extras on a film set, no one stepped within reach of the impassive new Chinese soldiers.
The British guards had been formidably friendly. The new Chinese regime was all business. There was no chit-chat.
That China has garrisoned Hong Kong with 5,000 of its finest soldiers from the People's Liberation Army could hardly be doubted from the discipline evident in their arrival.
Hundreds of PLA combat troops crossed into the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region riding in open-backed trucks at dawn on Tuesday morning.
They rode for miles in driving rain, standing to attention in the rear of the vehicles, staring neither left nor right but straight ahead.
As they entered the town of Sheung Shui, where a crowd of several thousand residents braved the downpour to welcome the troops, the PLA soldiers waved in response to cheers.
While the cheers were spontaneous, the waves were not. Each soldier moved his white gloved hand from left to right in a virtually identical arc, like a windscreen wiper.
There was no up-and-down waving, no circular motion, just a uniform, metronomic gesture which obviously had been the subject of extensive drill.
"It shows that the PLA leadership wrote a script for the entrance," said one Chinese man who watched the procession.
"Nothing has been left to chance. But that wave also tells me that these soldiers who would fire their weapons at us with the same sense of duty and discipline."
